before: order(keys, scores) returns row positions sorted by keys, breaking equal-key ties with scores. For this default ordering, unresolved ties retain their original relative order. Apply the same index to every aligned column; sorting one column alone breaks row relationships.

duplicated marks occurrences after the first equal value. It does not automatically merge or remove all rows belonging to repeated keys. To detect a nonunique key policy, use those flags deliberately rather than assuming sorting removes duplicates.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
keys <- c("b", "a", "a")
scores <- c(1, 3, 2)
i <- order(keys, scores)
cat(scores[i], "\n")
cat(duplicated(keys), "\n")
```

Expected output or behavior: 2 3 1
FALSE FALSE TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
keys <- c("b", "a", "a")
scores <- c(1, 3, 2)
i <- order(keys, scores)
cat(scores[i], "\n")
cat(duplicated(keys), "\n")
```
The output is `2 3 1`, then `FALSE FALSE TRUE`. The ordered scores are two, three, one. The separate duplicate check marks only the repeated a in the original keys.
Leave out the second sorting value and see how the tied entries keep their original order.
